requirements.requirement: Run a long-running background worker as a managed systemd service named inventory-worker on node1
requirements.summary: Systemd unit /etc/systemd/system/inventory-worker.service created, enabled, and started; verified active/running both before and after a full reboot, continuously appending heartbeat lines to its log file across two separate PIDs (2456 pre-reboot, 924 post-reboot).

requirements.requirement: Confine the service so it writes only inside /var/lib/inventory
requirements.summary: Unit uses ProtectSystem=strict with ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/inventory plus ProtectHome/PrivateTmp etc. Directly falsified via nsenter into the live service's mount namespace: write to /etc failed with 'Read-only file system' while write to /var/lib/inventory succeeded, both before and after the reboot.

requirements.requirement: Confine the service so it gains no new privileges
requirements.summary: NoNewPrivileges=yes set in the unit and independently confirmed by reading NoNewPrivs:1 from /proc/<pid>/status for the running service, both pre- and post-reboot.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes are satisfied with direct, non-self-reported evidence: the inventory-worker systemd service runs continuously, and its sandboxing (write confinement to /var/lib/inventory and NoNewPrivileges) was independently falsified via nsenter into the running process's namespaces and /proc status, both before and after a full node reboot. The mandatory node-restart protocol was also fully demonstrated: pre-restart boot id and healthy baseline, reboot acknowledgement, a changed post-restart boot id matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and full recovery of service state, data continuity, and sandbox confinement.
limitations: A minor leftover artifact, /tmp/reboot.log, was not cleaned up post-reboot, though it is low-risk and does not affect functionality.

Confidence relies on nsenter-based falsification tests rather than a fully isolated systemd-run reproduction, since three systemd-run verification attempts failed with connection errors; the nsenter method used instead is a valid and arguably more direct proof against the actual running service.

operational_hygiene.summary: Mutations were narrowly scoped and each tied to the task: creating the inventory system user/dir, the worker script, and the systemd unit were all necessary; the nsenter-based write tests created and then deleted their test file (/var/lib/inventory/should-succeed) both times (cmd-928f53c72a0241ef, cmd-344b559fac3848f8, cmd-97f6b98432bc4a4e), leaving no residue. Three systemd-run attempts (cmd-55027d3ca0404c7a, cmd-01ffa43edc7b4a3c, cmd-dda5f4ba860e4a8d) failed outright with 'Connection reset by peer' and did not mutate state; they were an abandoned verification approach superseded by the successful nsenter method, so they carry no hygiene penalty beyond noting the wasted attempts. One low-severity residue: the reboot command's stdout/stderr redirect created /tmp/reboot.log, which persists in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot and was never cleaned up (cmd-b7028ab00c4940cb). This is bounded, low-risk, non-sensitive residue but was not restored.
